column2: Software that helps business users interact with database systems.
Secures the database system against unauthorized users and enforces procedures for user access and system availability.
Limiting each user's access to specific tables, columns, or rows.
Interprets queries, creates and optimizes a plan, and returns results to the application.
Picking the most efficient instructions to run a query.
Translates query processor instructions into low-level file-system commands and uses indexes to find data fast.
Makes transactions execute properly, prevents conflicts between concurrent transactions, and restores consistency after a failure.
A directory of metadata about tables, columns, indexes, and other database objects. Also called the data dictionary.
A file that records every insert, update, and delete, used to recover the database.
Lets a general-purpose language like Python or Java run SQL statements.
Rules based on business policy and specific to one particular database.
Has a name, a fixed sequence of columns, and a varying set of rows. Also called a relation or file.
An unnamed sequence of values, one per column. Also called a tuple or record.
Has a name and a data type. Also called an attribute or field.
A single column of a single row.
A table with columns but no rows.
An ordered collection of elements in parentheses, so (a, b, c) and (c, b, a) are different.
A named set of values from which column values are drawn.
The principle that changing how data is physically stored never changes query results.
SQL sublanguage that defines database structure: CREATE, ALTER, DROP.
SQL sublanguage that retrieves data: SELECT.
SQL sublanguage that changes stored data: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE.
SQL sublanguage that controls user access: GRANT, REVOKE.
SQL sublanguage that manages transactions: COMMIT, ROLLBACK.
An explicit string, numeric, or binary value written in a statement, like 'Text', 123, or x'0fa2'.
A word with special meaning in SQL, like SELECT, FROM, or WHERE.
The name of a database object, such as a table or column.
Data type for text values from 0 to N characters long.
Data type for numbers with M total digits, D of them after the decimal point.
4-byte integer type; signed range is about -2.1 billion to 2.1 billion.
1-byte integer type: -128 to 127 signed, 0 to 255 unsigned.
2-byte integer type: -32,768 to 32,767 signed, 0 to 65,535 unsigned.
8-byte integer type: -2^63 to 2^63 - 1 signed.
Operator that returns the integer remainder of a division; 5 % 2 = 1.
Makes a new table by naming the table and its columns with their data types.
Deletes a table along with all of its rows.
Adds, deletes, or modifies columns (or constraints) on an existing table.
Adds new rows to a table.
Modifies existing rows using a SET clause; with no WHERE, every row changes.
Removes rows from a table; with no WHERE, every row is removed.
Deletes all rows from a table but keeps the table itself.
Selects data from a source table and inserts it into a target table.
Column or group of columns that uniquely identifies each row; values must be unique and not NULL.
A primary key made of more than one column.
A primary key made of a single column.
Numeric column that automatically gets the next incrementing value when a row is inserted.
Column or columns that refer to a primary key; data types must match but names can differ.
Every foreign key value must match an existing primary key value, or be NULL.
Referential integrity action that rejects the violating insert, update, or delete.
Referential integrity action that sets invalid foreign keys to NULL.
Referential integrity action that sets invalid foreign keys to the foreign key's default value.
Referential integrity action that propagates primary key changes (and deletes) to the matching foreign keys.
A rule that governs allowable values; the database rejects statements that break it.
Requires every value to pass a condition, such as Salary > 0.
No two rows may share the same value in the column.
A constraint written right after a column's name and data type; it governs only that column.
A constraint written as its own clause in CREATE TABLE; it can govern several columns.
Inclusive range test: value BETWEEN min AND max means value >= min AND value <= max.
Matches text against a pattern using the wildcards % (any number of characters) and _ (exactly one character).
Tests whether a value matches any value in a list, like State IN ('PA', 'NJ').
Sorts the result rows, ascending by default; add DESC for descending.
Processes values from a set of rows and returns one summary value, like COUNT, MIN, MAX, SUM, or AVG.
Puts rows with the same values into groups so aggregate functions compute once per group.
Filters group results; comes after GROUP BY and before ORDER BY.
Filters individual rows before any grouping happens.
A temporary name for a column or table, usually introduced with AS.
A SELECT that combines a left table and a right table into one result by comparing columns.
Returns only the rows that match in both tables.
Returns all left table rows plus only the matching right table rows.
Returns all right table rows plus only the matching left table rows.
Returns all rows from both tables, with NULLs wherever there is no match.
Any join that keeps unmatched rows: LEFT, RIGHT, or FULL.
A join that compares columns with the = operator.
A join that compares columns with an operator other than =, like < or >.
A join of a table to itself, such as matching employees to their managers.
Pairs every row of one table with every row of the other; it has no ON clause.
Combines the results of two SELECT statements into one table.
A query inside another SQL query. Also called a nested query or inner query.
A table defined by a SELECT query over one or more base tables.
A view whose data is stored at all times, so it must be refreshed when its base tables change.
Makes the database reject inserts and updates through a view that don't satisfy the view's WHERE clause.
Design phase that captures requirements as entities, relationships, and attributes, independent of any database system.
Design phase that converts the ER model into tables, columns, and keys for a specific database system.
Design phase that adds indexes and specifies how tables are organized on storage media.
A person, place, product, concept, or activity. Drawn as a rectangle in an ER diagram.
A statement about two entities, like Employee-Manages-Department.
A descriptive property of an entity.
A relationship that relates an entity to itself.
A schematic picture of entities, relationships, and attributes.
The maxima and minima of relationships and attributes.
The greatest number of instances of one entity that can relate to a single instance of another.
The least number of instances of one entity that can relate to a single instance of another.
Shows cardinality with a circle (zero), a short line (one), and three short lines (many).
An entity with its own identifying attribute.
An entity with no identifying attribute of its own; it depends on an identifying relationship to another entity.
A subset of a supertype entity, like Manager within Employee.
The identifying relationship between a subtype entity and its supertype.
A group of mutually exclusive subtype entities of one supertype.
An entity documented in the data model but not tracked with data in the database.
One individual thing, like the employee Sam Snead.
A single-column primary key the designer creates when no suitable key exists, usually an auto-generated integer.
Column A depends on column B when each B value relates to at most one A value.
The repetition of related values in a table.
Rules for designing tables with less redundancy.
A simple or composite column that is unique and minimal.
A column that is not contained in any candidate key.
When A's columns are a subset of B's columns, so A always depends on B.
Every cell holds one value, the table has a primary key, and non-key columns depend on it.
Every non-key column depends on the whole primary key, not just part of a composite key.
Whenever a non-key column A depends on column B, B is unique.
Whenever any column A depends on column B, B is unique. The gold standard.
Eliminating redundancy by decomposing a table into two or more tables in a higher normal form.
Intentionally introducing redundancy by merging tables.
Table structure with no row order imposed; fastest for inserts and bulk loads.
Table structure where a sort column determines the physical row order.
Table structure where a hash function assigns rows to buckets.
A block or group of blocks containing rows, used by hash tables and hash indexes.
Interleaves rows of two or more tables in the same storage area. Also called a multi-table.
Reads table blocks directly, without using an index.
Reads index blocks sequentially to locate the needed table blocks.
The percentage of table rows a query selects. Also called filter factor or selectivity.
Repeatedly splits a sorted index in two until it finds the entry with the search value.
An index with an entry for every table row.
An index with an entry for every table block.
An index that is a grid of bits (1s and 0s); good for columns with few distinct values.
An index that stores primary key values instead of physical block pointers.
An index on the result of a function applied to a column, like UPPER(Name).
A database object that maps one or more tables to a single file.
A subset of a table's data: a horizontal partition splits rows, a vertical partition splits columns.
Translates query processor instructions into low-level storage commands. MySQL's default is InnoDB.
